title: RSI under 30 won 76% of its trades on SPY over 25 years and still sat through a 31% drawdown
author: person-person12
selftext:
Buy when RSI drops under 30 is probably the first rule anybody gets taught, and right behind it comes the idea that a high win rate means the system works. I had never seen those two put against each other with a real number, so i ran it on SPY daily candles from January 2001 to the end of March 2026, ten grand, commission and slippage charged on both sides of every fill.

The rules and nothing else in them. Buy at the close when RSI(14) closes under 30, sell at the close when RSI closes back above 50. No stop, no target, no trend filter.

* 140 trades
* **76.4% win rate**
* profit factor 2.09
* net **+202.3%**, ten grand to $30,230
* max drawdown **31.4%**

It made money, which wasnt what i expected going in. The part i'd be careful with is the 76%. Three out of four trades closing green is the number ppl quote when theyre defending a system, and on this one its doing almost none of the work, because the damage sits entirely in the handful that went the other way.

The worst trade in the run opened on the 31st of August 2001 and closed a month later down $792 against a ten thousand dollar account. RSI went under 30 and price just kept going, and because there is no stop in these rules the position stayed open the whole way down.

The SPY history i ran this on in [Agenticks](https://www.agenticks.ca/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=autopilot&utm_content=ai_trading) starts in January 2001, so the window carries the dot com unwind and 2008 instead of stopping somewhere convenient. 33 of the 140 trades were losers and those 33 carried the entire 31.4% drawdown.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Good that the window includes 2001 and 2008, and that you point out the 76% win rate tells you little by itself. One thing I'd add is the comparison to buy and hold over the same dates, plus time in the market, since that's where a rule like this usually looks different. The 140 trades are also clustered in a few selloffs, so the number of independent episodes is much smaller. Tagging them by cause, such as rate shocks or crises, would help, and Cymetica's EventTrader is one source of event timing for that.
